sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

matches.title: Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights
matches.abstract_excerpt: Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional $\ell_2$ weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with $124$M to $500$M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At $500$M and a $4\%$ distortion budget, it reaches $1.89\times$ compression and $1.18\times$ GPU inference speedup, compared with $1.14\times$ and $1.01\times$ after standard weight decay. matches.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
matches.abstract_excerpt: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. matches.abstract_excerpt: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. matches.title: ORCA: The Annealed Spectral Conditioning Optimizer for Faster, Better LLM Training
matches.abstract_excerpt: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. matches.title: How Finite-Rank Bottlenecks Shape the Low-Rank Adaptation Landscape
matches.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. matches.title: MLoRA:Continual Low-Rank Adaptation via Relative-Response Subspace Selection and Momentum Orthogonalization
matches.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) provides a parameter-efficient approach to continual learning, but its nominal rank can conceal a loss of effective adaptation capacity. This exposes a limitation of interference avoidance alone: protecting historical representations does not ensure that the remaining adaptation capacity is responsive to new tasks or effectively utilized. matches.title: Rotated Manifold Optimization for Low-Rank Adaptation
matches.abstract_excerpt: We propose a novel optimizer for low-rank adaptation (LoRA) that explicitly incorporates the gauge symmetry of low-rank factorization. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.

matches.title: A KAN-based Non-linear Factorization for Embedding Layer Compression
matches.abstract_excerpt: Among existing embedding compression approaches, low-rank factorization provides a simple and mathematically principled solution by approximating the embedding matrix with a reduced-rank decomposition. To overcome these limitations, we propose an enhanced factorization scheme that increases expressive power by introducing learnable non-linear projections within the compressed embedding layer. matches.title: Frozen Factor or Spectral Band? Disentangling Two Choices in Low-Rank LoRA
matches.abstract_excerpt: Spectral variants of low-rank adaptation (LoRA) choose both a subspace and which factor to freeze. We separate these choices by freezing the input factor A or output factor B on the top or bottom singular directions of pretrained weights, with learning rates selected separately. At rank 2, the same-band advantage of freezing A is larger than either within-factor band difference on all four task-model pairs with complete comparisons. Freezing B also trails comparable-budget free LoRA by 8-18 percentage points on five pairs spanning a formatting task and OpenBookQA. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

For the 500 500 M model and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it supports 1.89 × 1.89\times compression, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times after standard weight decay. Pretraining is expensive, motivating methods that prepare existing checkpoints for compression during a short fine-tuning stage. Substantial rank reduction without loss of model quality remains difficult. We compare spectral weight decay during pretraining with its use after pretraining from a standard ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay checkpoint. The 124 124 M-parameter model is pretrained for one Chinchilla-optimal training budget [ Hoffmann et al., 2022 ] , then fine-tuned on 32.8 32.8 M tokens. Appendix B.2 compares spectral weight decay with the fine-tuning method Prehab [ Qin et al., 2025 ] .

The main experiments use Adam-family optimizers. Its decoupled correction can be applied to the candidate weights produced by any optimizer, but the resulting loss and rank dynamics depend on the optimizer. Figure 6 : Optimizer-dependent loss and rank dynamics. The top row shows validation loss, and the bottom row shows mean effective rank. The columns compare ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay with coefficient 0.1 0.1 across optimizers, spectral regularization with Muon, and spectral regularization with Lion. Colors match between the loss and rank panels. Figure 6 (a,d) compares optimizers with the same ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay coefficient of 0.1 0.1 . The Muon sweep in Figure 6 (b,e) shows that substantial rank reduction comes with a steep validation-loss increase, limiting the practical appeal of this combination. By contrast, Lion exhibits a more favorable trade-off between loss and rank in Figure 6 (c,f), qualitatively similar to Adam.

A mean effective rank of about 300 300 requires λ = 0.8 \lambda=0.8 for Adam, λ = 0.4 \lambda=0.4 for Muon, and λ = 4 \lambda=4 for Lion. inspect:2610.22794.question: In the 1B LLaMA pretraining experiments, what are Ori’s measured peak GPU memory, training throughput or step time, and validation-loss results versus GaLore and other low-rank optimizer baselines under matched rank and training budgets?

passages.text: We thus introduce Ori , a streaming k k -PCA-based O ja-style updated low- r ank i terative optimizer, designed to exploit the slow-drift regime of LLM gradient subspaces. Rather than treating each subspace estimation as an independent, “cold-start” problem—as is the case with periodic SVD recomputation in GaLore—Ori treats subspace estimation as a continuous tracking problem. The core innovation of Ori lies in its drift-aware bootstrapping mechanism: we carry over (transfer) the subspace basis from previous steps as the initialization state for the current step. Because of the slow-drift phenomenon, the prior basis provides a suitable starting point that requires only a few lightweight, streaming k k -PCA-inspired updates to realign with the instantaneous gradient geometry. In practice, Ori instantiates this via the Oja++ algorithm [ 24 , 1 ] , which enables high-frequency basis rotations at a per-step cost of only 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ​ k 2 ) \mathcal{O}(dk^{2}) . This approach allows for a warm-start transfer of Adam-style first and second moments between successive bases, ensuring stable optimization dynamics. Beyond computational efficiency, we show that this formulation allows Ori to achieve provable sublinear dynamic regret bounds under drift, providing new theoretical tools and guarantees for tracking fidelity that static recomputation methods lack.

Empirically, Ori narrowly tracks the evolving gradient subspace and converts this tracking fidelity into end-to-end wins where it matters most: very low ranks. Under tight rank budgets, each dimension in the projector is precious, and stale misalignment is especially costly. Empirical results show that Ori reduces the performance gap of state-of-the-art low-rank baselines to the full-rank Adam optimizer by up to 69.3% on the 1B LLaMA pre-training task, where the optimizer state rank is 128 in contrast to the model embedding dimension of 2048. And on Roberta-Base fine-tuning tasks, where the ranks are even lower (8 or 4), Ori achieves superior performance on 10 out of 16 scenarios. Moreover, Ori achieved this superior performance with one of the lowest computation budgets. See Figure 1 for a performance–memory overview on LLaMA-1B pre-training, where Ori consistently sits on the bottom-left frontier. Through ablation, we observe that (i) increasing the projector-update period degrades performance—quantifying the cost of staleness, and (ii) injecting a small carry-over (via a drift coefficient ρ ≈ 0.99 \rho\approx 0.99 ) improves accuracy—confirming the value of continuity and statistic transfer. Across pre-training and fine-tuning settings, Ori consistently improves the performance–memory trade-off over LoRA, GaLore, and OSD in the low-rank regime, thereby reducing the gap to full-rank Adam. Our primary contributions in this work are as follows: • We identify and quantify slow gradient subspace drift during LLM training and argue that exploiting its continuity – not merely reacting to it – matters for low-rank optimization.

passages.section: E.8 Measuring optimizer state peak memory
passages.text: Finally, we report our procedure for measuring the memory footprint of the optimizers evaluated in our experiments. Our goal is to record the peak memory usage, incurred solely by the said optimizer’s update step. To this end, we take advantage of PyTorch’s memory recording functionalities. The below code listing shows the pseudocode for recording peack memory usage incurred solely by the optimizer’s step() operations. We use this procedure to obtain all the results in Tables 9 and 11 . Python code for profiling optimizer peak memory. ⬇ import torch # Model and optimizer setup model = … optimizer = … # Main training loop for batch in enumerate ( dataloader ): # Forward and backward pass loss = model (** batch ). loss loss . backward () # Record the current memory usage after model backward mem_after_backward = torch . cuda . memory_allocated () # Reset the max memory counter torch . cuda . reset_peak_memory_stats () # Optimizer step optimizer . step () # Read the optimizer-incurred max memory # The difference with mem_after_backward is the # maximum additional memory caused by optimizer.step() peak_mem_during_step = torch . cuda . max_memory_allocated () optim_peak_mem = peak_mem_during_step - mem_after_backward

We thus introduce Ori , a streaming k k -PCA-based O ja-style updated low- r ank i terative optimizer, designed to exploit the slow-drift regime of LLM gradient subspaces. Rather than treating each subspace estimation as an independent, “cold-start” problem—as is the case with periodic SVD recomputation in GaLore—Ori treats subspace estimation as a continuous tracking problem. The core innovation of Ori lies in its drift-aware bootstrapping mechanism: we carry over (transfer) the subspace basis from previous steps as the initialization state for the current step. Because of the slow-drift phenomenon, the prior basis provides a suitable starting point that requires only a few lightweight, streaming k k -PCA-inspired updates to realign with the instantaneous gradient geometry. In practice, Ori instantiates this via the Oja++ algorithm [ 24 , 1 ] , which enables high-frequency basis rotations at a per-step cost of only 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ​ k 2 ) \mathcal{O}(dk^{2}) . This approach allows for a warm-start transfer of Adam-style first and second moments between successive bases, ensuring stable optimization dynamics. Beyond computational efficiency, we show that this formulation allows Ori to achieve provable sublinear dynamic regret bounds under drift, providing new theoretical tools and guarantees for tracking fidelity that static recomputation methods lack.

Empirically, Ori narrowly tracks the evolving gradient subspace and converts this tracking fidelity into end-to-end wins where it matters most: very low ranks. Under tight rank budgets, each dimension in the projector is precious, and stale misalignment is especially costly. Empirical results show that Ori reduces the performance gap of state-of-the-art low-rank baselines to the full-rank Adam optimizer by up to 69.3% on the 1B LLaMA pre-training task, where the optimizer state rank is 128 in contrast to the model embedding dimension of 2048. And on Roberta-Base fine-tuning tasks, where the ranks are even lower (8 or 4), Ori achieves superior performance on 10 out of 16 scenarios. Moreover, Ori achieved this superior performance with one of the lowest computation budgets. See Figure 1 for a performance–memory overview on LLaMA-1B pre-training, where Ori consistently sits on the bottom-left frontier. Through ablation, we observe that (i) increasing the projector-update period degrades performance—quantifying the cost of staleness, and (ii) injecting a small carry-over (via a drift coefficient ρ ≈ 0.99 \rho\approx 0.99 ) improves accuracy—confirming the value of continuity and statistic transfer. Across pre-training and fine-tuning settings, Ori consistently improves the performance–memory trade-off over LoRA, GaLore, and OSD in the low-rank regime, thereby reducing the gap to full-rank Adam. Our primary contributions in this work are as follows: • We identify and quantify slow gradient subspace drift during LLM training and argue that exploiting its continuity – not merely reacting to it – matters for low-rank optimization.

Finally, we report our procedure for measuring the memory footprint of the optimizers evaluated in our experiments. Our goal is to record the peak memory usage, incurred solely by the said optimizer’s update step. To this end, we take advantage of PyTorch’s memory recording functionalities. The below code listing shows the pseudocode for recording peack memory usage incurred solely by the optimizer’s step() operations. We use this procedure to obtain all the results in Tables 9 and 11 . Python code for profiling optimizer peak memory. ⬇ import torch # Model and optimizer setup model = … optimizer = … # Main training loop for batch in enumerate ( dataloader ): # Forward and backward pass loss = model (** batch ). loss loss . backward () # Record the current memory usage after model backward mem_after_backward = torch . cuda . memory_allocated () # Reset the max memory counter torch . cuda . reset_peak_memory_stats () # Optimizer step optimizer . step () # Read the optimizer-incurred max memory # The difference with mem_after_backward is the # maximum additional memory caused by optimizer.step() peak_mem_during_step = torch . cuda . max_memory_allocated () optim_peak_mem = peak_mem_during_step - mem_after_backward

inspect:2610.23571.question: In the practical Transformer experiments, does BMuon improve low-rank SVD weight compression or only structured channel pruning? What matched model-quality, compression, and training-compute results are reported versus Muon?

passages.text: NuMuon ( Dolatabadi et al., 2026 ) is the closest prior compression-aware variant of Muon. It imposes a nuclear-norm constraint on Muon’s update direction to improve low-rank compressibility. BMuon instead targets structured compressibility over hidden channels by introducing a global channel budget into Muon’s spectral-norm geometry. Prior work has also incorporated compressibility into training. Lu et al. (2022) train networks for unstructured pruning with Frank–Wolfe under fixed layerwise constraints on the weights, while Zimmer et al. (2025) use Frank–Wolfe under fixed norm constraints for convolutional filter pruning and low-rank compression. BMuon instead leaves the weights unconstrained and modifies Muon’s spectral update geometry for global hidden-channel compression. Resource-constrained structure learning and global structured pruning have been studied across CNNs and Transformers ( Gordon et al., 2018 ; Yu et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; An et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . GRASPrune ( Wang et al., 2026b ) learns gates post hoc on a frozen LLM to select MLP channels and attention KV-head groups under a single global parameter budget, while DABP ( Laroui et al., 2026 ) jointly trains CNN weights and continuous channel gates under a global resource budget. BMuon uses no forward gates; its budget instead controls the channel-wise reweighting of Muon’s spectral update constraint during training.

We first test whether BMuon produces models that can be compressed directly after training without post-compression fine-tuning. We train a small Vision Transformer on CIFAR-100 for 200 epochs over three seeds. We compare Muon, Muon with a proximal Group-Lasso penalty on coupled MLP channels (Muon+GL) ( Yuan and Lin, 2006 ; Wen et al., 2016 ) , NuMuon ( Dolatabadi et al., 2026 ) , and BMuon. NuMuon is particularly relevant as a direct comparison: it modifies the Muon update to improve compressibility, but targets low-rank structure through the singular spectrum, whereas BMuon targets structured MLP-channel compression. BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and a budget annealed to 20 % 20\% of the total MLP-channel mass. Full experimental details in Appendix E.2 .

Figure 2 shows the post-training fragility that motivates this work: Muon falls to 5.72 % 5.72\% test accuracy after only 30 % 30\% MLP-channel pruning. Muon+GL remains robust through 50 % 50\% pruning, while NuMuon degrades more gradually under low-rank compression. Under magnitude-based pruning, BMuon is substantially more compressible than the structured baselines while matching Muon’s dense accuracy: BMuon reaches 71.46 % 71.46\% , versus 71.49 % 71.49\% for Muon, 71.25 % 71.25\% for Muon+GL, and 69.95 % 69.95\% for NuMuon. Using μ \mu for ranking provides a further gain: at 80 % 80\% pruning, BM- μ \mu retains 70.57 % 70.57\% accuracy, compared with 60.84 % 60.84\% for BM-mag, while Muon, Muon+GL, and NuMuon have fallen to 1.93 % 1.93\% , 6.01 % 6.01\% , and 3.84 % 3.84\% , respectively. The advantage of BM-mag under the shared magnitude criterion isolates the compressibility benefit of BMuon training, while the further gain from BM- μ \mu indicates that the learned allocation also carries useful channel-importance information.

Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply under post-training MLP-channel pruning, motivating the question of whether Muon’s spectral geometry can be modified to favor structured compressibility. BMuon addresses this question by reweighting hidden channels within Muon’s spectral-norm constraints and making them compete for a global budget. We show that the resulting norm family recovers Muon and connects it to channel-sparse geometries. In linear two-factor models, Muon admits minimum-cost factorizations with redundant hidden width, whereas under a sufficiently scarce BMuon budget every minimum-cost factorization is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a tractable minorization–maximization approximation to the global allocation oracle. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

At evaluation, NuMuon compresses only the 12 MLP weight matrices using truncated SVD; attention weights remain dense. We distribute the retained rank budget as evenly as possible across matrices, with minimum rank 4. At each compression level, we choose the NuMuon rank so that the resulting whole-model parameter count is as close as possible to that of the corresponding structured-pruned model. Table 5 reports the exact post-training compression results corresponding to Fig. 2 . Table 5 : CIFAR-100 post-training compression results. Test accuracy (%) reported as mean ± \pm sample standard deviation over three seeds. All compression levels are evaluated independently from the final epoch-200 checkpoint, without post-compression fine-tuning.

matches.title: Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights
matches.abstract_excerpt: Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional $\ell_2$ weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with $124$M to $500$M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At $500$M and a $4\%$ distortion budget, it reaches $1.89\times$ compression and $1.18\times$ GPU inference speedup, compared with $1.14\times$ and $1.01\times$ after standard weight decay. matches.title: Convergence of Practical Muon with Finite Newton-Schulz Iterations and Nesterov Momentum
matches.abstract_excerpt: Practical Muon maintains momentum and performs a small, fixed number of Newton--Schulz iterations separately for each parameter matrix, often with a Nesterov correction. passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.

Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Most existing theory addresses nearby questions through linearization or simplified training dynamics. In the NTK regime, Jang et al. (2024) shows that full fine-tuning admits a low-rank solution and that sufficiently overparameterized LoRA eliminates spurious local minima. Afzal et al. (2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. (2025) study LoRA dynamics and prove a dichotomy between convergence to a low-rank global minimizer and convergence to a qualitatively different high-rank solution. These works are complementary to ours, but they do not answer a more structural question: what property of the objective function makes low-rank optima available in the first place?

• Low-rank representer theorem for trace-norm fine-tuning. For a frozen network in which an adapted block T T is observed only through a finite-rank linear map Φ ⁡ ( T ) \Phi(T) of bottleneck rank d Φ d_{\Phi} , we prove that the trace-norm-regularized problem has a global minimizer whose rank is controlled by d Φ d_{\Phi} ; see Theorem 4.1 . The multi-stage extension is Theorem 4.3 . • Rank bounds from attention invariances. For multi-head attention, query and key updates are observable only through centered score subspaces because row-wise softmax is invariant to row-wise additive constants. Value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. Combining these invariances with projector compression gives the optimizer-dependent subspace rank bounds in Theorem 4.4 . • Generic first-order rank deficiency for factorized LoRA. For the weight-decayed LoRA factorization, we prove that after a generic positive semidefinite perturbation, full-column-rank first-order stationary points are excluded whenever the Pataki–Barvinok rank threshold exceeds the dimension of the associated family of symmetric KKT matrices; see Theorem 4.7 . The multistage and attention consequence are Theorem C.9 and Corollary 4.8 . This is a first-order exclusion theorem, not a no-spurious-local-minima theorem; Proposition 4.9 gives an explicit limitation. • Perturbation transfer and generalization. We show that global minimizers of the perturbed factorized objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm-regularized problem when the perturbation is small; see Theorem 4.10 .

inspect:2610.10965.question: In the NanoGPT experiments, how do the spectrally targeted variants compare with standard Muon on validation loss, training compute, and effective rank of weight matrices? Which singular directions drive the reported differences?

passages.text: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

The Muon optimizer for deep learning works by orthogonalizing the update matrix ( Jordan et al., 2024b ) . Unlike many other proposed optimizers, this has been highly successful empirically for training large language models, especially when coupled with weight decay ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . This is because the matrix can be orthogonalized relatively efficiently, using methods such as Newton-Schulz or Polar Express ( Amsel et al., 2026 ) . The orthogonalization step can be thought of as applying the matrix sign function to the gradient matrix, which normalizes all the singular values to one, prompting the question of whether Muon’s success comes from amplifying small but important directions with small singular values ignored by standard gradient descent, or from normalizing large, degenerate directions with large singular values that misdirect the training. The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. inspect:2611.17191.question: In the language-model LoRA experiments, what matched-rank baselines, learning-rate tuning, seeds, model scales, perplexity results, and training-time or memory overhead are reported for the Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

inspect:2610.04204.question: For LLaMA pretraining, what matched-budget validation-loss, peak GPU training memory, optimizer-state memory, and wall-clock results does Clean or Q-Clean report versus AdamW, Muon, and SOAP?

passages.text: Training large language models (LLMs) entails a fundamental trade-off: memory-efficient optimizers such as Adam discard cross-parameter curvature, whereas full-curvature methods such as SOAP can accelerate convergence at prohibitive memory costs. We introduce Clean , a memory-efficient and full-curvature optimizer designed to resolve this bottleneck. Clean leverages the randomized Nyström method to accurately approximate the left and right preconditioners in SOAP, and to reduce the optimizer’s memory complexity from quadratic to linear in terms of model dimensions. We subsequently reintegrate the off-subspace components to capture curvature information beyond the low-rank approximation, preserving rich curvature at minimal memory cost. We further propose Q-Clean , a low-precision variant that aggressively compresses optimizer states. Q-Clean reduces optimizer memory consumption by over 50% compared to Muon when pre-training a LLaMA-1.3B architecture, all while maintaining strong and competitive predictive performance. Notably, Clean operates with a smaller optimizer-state footprint than standard AdamW while reaching AdamW’s final performance 26% faster in wall-clock time. Furthermore, our methods uniquely enable the pre-training of a 13B-parameter model on a single 80GB GPU, providing a scalable, efficient, and accessible approach to large-scale model optimization. $*$ $*$ footnotetext: Equal contribution.

We compare against AdamW ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) , SOAP ( Vyas et al., 2024 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , and ALSO ( Romashov et al., 2026 ) . At 350M we sweep three learning rates per method and report the best run in Table 3 . Due to the prohibitive cost of a full sweep at 1.3B, we performed a shortened sweep and resumed only the best configurations to 5,000 steps. Clean, Q-Clean and ALSO all use rank r = 256 r=256 at 350M and r = 512 r=512 at 1.3B, and all preconditioned methods refresh their preconditioner every T = 10 T=10 steps. Table 3: Final validation perplexity ( ↓ \downarrow ) and optimizer memory when pre-training LLaMA models of different sizes. Clean achieves competitive perplexity compared to full SOAP, while using less memory than AdamW. Clean, Q-Clean and ALSO use rank r = 256 r=256 at 350M and r = 512 r=512 at 1.3B. Excluding SOAP, the best results are shown in bold and the second best are underlined . Methods LLaMA-350M LLaMA-1.3B Perplexity Opt. Mem. Peak Mem. Perplexity Opt. Mem. Peak Mem. Table 3 summarizes the final results, demonstrating that Clean achieves competitive performance compared to SOAP, at a fraction of its cost. Q-Clean cuts the optimizer state memory consumption by more than 50% compared to Muon, and still delivers results on par with the full-rank methods. Fig. 4 plots validation perplexity throughout training for LLaMA-1.3B, where Clean follows SOAP closely and presents on-par results.

Clean’s memory advantage grows with scale (Figs. 7 and 8 ) because its memory complexity scales linearly with matrix dimensions, at a fixed rank r r , whereas every baseline carries at least one quadratic term (Table 2 ). Furthermore, Fig. 7 demonstrates a reduction in per-parameter memory cost as model size increases. See Appendix D for more details. (a) Validation loss against wall-clock time. (b) Steps to reach AdamW’s final loss. Figure 5: Convergence efficiency on pre-training LLaMA-1.3B, all runs on four H100 GPUs with the same batch size, schedule and token budget. (a) Wall-clock: Clean reaches AdamW’s final validation loss in 64 64 of the 81 81 hours of AdamW requirements, demonstrating 26% speedup. (b) Token efficiency: Clean reaches that loss in 77 % 77\% of the training budget and Q-Clean in 87 % 87\% . To evaluate sample efficiency and convergence, Fig. 5 compares the methods across time and token budgets rather than focusing solely on the final loss. Clean reaches AdamW’s final performance in 64 hours instead of 81, while simultaneously reducing the optimizer memory footprint. inspect:2610.04507.question: In the 7B language-model and four vision-backbone label-noise experiments, what are the matched-rank LoRA versus dense fine-tuning controls, noise levels, seeds, and measured clean-test generalization results? Does the second-descent finding hold for the language model as well as vision models?

passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

passages.section: 5.3 The parameter-saving window closes before the descent arrives
passages.text: Every measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters carries higher risk than dense fine-tuning of the same projections, on DeiT-Tiny, ViT-Tiny and DeiT-Small, in every seed at a shared learning rate (Figure 2 b, Table 1 , Appendix C.1 ). The descent itself is genuine, since the DeiT-Tiny and ViT-Tiny sweeps keep falling past the peak once extended to 4 ​ d 4d ; what the paired column adds is its price, a gap that narrows only from above and only slowly, so wherever it closes at all it closes far outside the range where the adapter was still cheaper than dense. Inside the window. We sample five ranks between the peak and r parity r_{\mathrm{parity}} on DeiT-Tiny and three on ViT-Tiny, five seeds each, since those are the only points where a recovery could still retain a parameter advantage (Appendix C.1 ). None reaches dense. The paired gap remains between + 0.084 +0.084 and + 0.140 +0.140 nats, roughly four to seven times its seed-to-seed spread, and every seed agrees in sign on both NLL and accuracy. Giving each arm its own learning rate, selected on three seeds, narrows these gaps without closing them: re-run on ten fresh seeds, DeiT-Tiny’s r = 128 r{=}128 trails dense by + 0.062 +0.062 nats ( 95 % 95\% t t -interval [ + 0.026 , + 0.099 ] [+0.026,+0.099] , nine of ten seeds), and ViT-Tiny’s trails by + 0.065 +0.065 on every selection seed (Appendix C.2 ). We have measured the window in which a recovery could still match dense while saving parameters, and it is empty.

passages.text: Outside the window. At r expr r_{\mathrm{expr}} , where either adapter can already express any dense weight update, both backbones remain behind dense. Under the shared rate, DeiT-Tiny passes a paired equivalence test with two one-sided tests (TOST) against a 0.05 0.05 -nat margin, a tenth of the cliff’s depth, first at r = 3 ​ d r{=}3d (eight seeds), four times dense’s projection-weight count; ViT-Tiny does not pass it there. With each arm at its own best rate, dense gains from a higher rate while LoRA’s best at 3 ​ d 3d is the shared one, so the difference there becomes + 0.031 +0.031 nats, positive in every seed but inside the margin (Appendix C.2 ); the equivalence at 3 ​ d 3d is established only under the shared rate. The same shortfall at 7 7 B. To test the finding at language-model scale, we repeat the measurement on Qwen2.5-7B ( Qwen Team, 2024 ) over 5,000 5{,}000 AG News examples ( Zhang et al., 2015 ) with 20 % 20\% label noise, adapting the qkv projections of the last six blocks at twelve ranks up to d = 3584 d{=}3584 against dense fine-tuning of the same modules ( 3 3 shared seeds; Appendix C.3 ). Grouped-query attention makes the projections cheap relative to the adapter and places parity at r ≈ 1075 r{\approx}1075 , which we sample, so this axis is the clean test of the two references in Equation 1 . They part company sharply (Figure 3 ). At r = 448 r{=}448 the valley reference reads Rec = 1.06 \mathrm{Rec}{=}1.06 , a second descent that has already completed, while the dense reference puts the same point 0.058 0.058 nats short, and G G remains positive at every measured rank and in every seed, parity included. Read against a valley this sweep recovers fully; read against dense it never arrives.

passages.text: Figure 3: One rank, two references. Qwen2.5-7B, three-seed means (Appendix C.3 ). Table 1: Post-peak test NLL and the gap to dense fine-tuning. We compare LoRA ranks up to 4 ​ d 4d with dense fine-tuning of the same qkv projections in the same six blocks, under the shared learning rate; the arms share seeds, subsets and noise draws. Params is the trainable projection-weight count relative to dense, so parity falls at r = 0.75 ​ d r{=}0.75d , and r = 128 r{=}128 is one of the post-peak ranks sampled below it (Appendix C.1 ). Paired diff. is the mean per-seed difference, with a 95 % 95\% bootstrap interval over five or eight shared seeds and a descriptive three-seed range otherwise. Dense is the eight-seed mean; its five- and three-seed means are 1.971 1.971 / 1.977 1.977 on DeiT-Tiny and 1.796 1.796 / 1.810 1.810 on ViT-Tiny.

Model selection shrinks the cliff without removing it. Selecting learning rate, weight decay and stopping epoch on a clean validation split reduces the cliff from 0.53 0.53 to 0.16 0.16 nats. The selected models retain the rank ordering on fresh seeds, and every selected checkpoint precedes interpolation (Appendix E.2 ), which is the mechanism: selection escapes the cliff by declining to interpolate, not by crossing it. Because per-rank selection includes no dense arm, it bears on the shape of the axis and not on the gap to dense. No tested setting removes the cliff once ranks interpolate. Corrupting the frozen backbone only deepens the cliff, and its shape persists through changes in data size, learning rate, weight decay, scaling, adapter placement and dataset (Appendices C.2 , E.1 and E.3 ; Table 15 ). Architecture decides too. A ResNet completes the descent on these subsets; a width-scaled ViT trained from scratch does not (Appendix B.2 ), recovering 0.56 0.56 of 3.23 3.23 nats, the final-ascent regime of Xue et al. (2024) . Dense-block fine-tuning of a transformer reaches Rec = 0.82 \mathrm{Rec}{=}0.82 , so the rank axis’s shallow far side is not a transformer property. Scope. The experiments cover noisy image and text classification with AdamW, synthetic and human label noise, and budgets up to 160 160 epochs. The dense reference is module-matched, training the projections LoRA adapts rather than the whole network; the dense-block axis of Section 5.5 unfreezes up to six full blocks. Test NLL is the primary measurement, and accuracy follows its ordering inside the parameter-saving window but can diverge at larger ranks. Where LoRA crosses dense depends on the protocol and the grid.

The rank axis does run a second descent, and a sweep that stops at full rank can miss it. Judging what this descent is worth requires a reference point, which the module-matched rank sweep supplies by grading every setting against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules with the trainable-parameter ratio beside it. Across four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model, no measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters reaches dense, and the first equivalence result sits at four times dense’s projection weights under a single shared learning rate. Full rank supplies the expressivity, so the remaining gap is a matter of coordinates, which the frozen-factor interventions show can move risk by about the size of the gap. LoRA’s parameter advantage is strongest at the cheap end and runs out in the tail; rank-one LoRA dominates dense outright on three of the four vision backbones. Rank keeps shaping generalization long after it stops saving parameters.

inspect:2611.07859.question: In the controlled closed-search comparisons, what are CORE’s measured answer-accuracy and evidence-recall results versus the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, and what retrieval corpus, agent-tool interface, and context-management mechanisms determine whether it is useful for a handwritten scientific-paper digest harness?

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

Our CORE harness, illustrated in Figure 1 , manages tool execution and context construction for a language model agent performing deep research. The agent decides what information to seek, and the harness retrieves and presents the corresponding evidence. We consider a closed-search setting over a fixed collection 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . Although this setting abstracts away the dynamics of the live web, it enables reproducible evaluation and controlled comparisons across agent models, retrieval backends, and harnesses. The agent follows a ReAct-style interaction loop ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Conditioned on the original question and the evidence accumulated in its context, the agent iteratively formulates sub-queries for the search interface and uses the returned evidence to guide subsequent searches or finalize the answer. Given the question x x , let I I denote the system instructions and tool descriptions. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. inspect:2610.04249.question: What balance and alignment assumptions support the singular-mode predictions for GD, SignGD, Muon, Shampoo, and K-FAC, and what experiments test those predictions beyond deep matrix factorization, especially on Transformer weights or LLM pretraining?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

We investigate these questions in deep linear networks, where depth changes the parameterization and optimization dynamics without changing the end-to-end linear functions. This makes it a particularly clean setting for separating optimizer-induced dynamics from parameterization-induced bias. Our theoretical analysis focuses on deep matrix factorization, a canonical special case in which the evolution of singular modes can be characterized explicitly. Specifically, in full observation regression, it exposes transient singular mode learning ( Saxe et al., 2013 ; Soudry et al., 2018 ) , while in underdetermined matrix sensing and completion, it permits direct study of which interpolating matrix is selected ( Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Rhee et al., 2026 ; Parviz et al., 2026 ) .

In contrast to the Euclidean geometry of GD, non-Euclidean optimizers transform the factorization-induced geometry in qualitatively different ways. SignGD and Adam apply coordinate-wise adaptive scaling ( Bernstein et al., 2018 ; Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) ; Muon acts directly on the spectrum of matrix updates ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) while Shampoo introduces history-dependent matrix preconditioning ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) ; and K-FAC attempts to compensate for the parameterization through curvature using approximate natural gradients ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ) . In our study, we categorize these geometries based on their updates into Euclidean (GD), coordinate-wise (SignGD and Adam), spectral (Muon and Shampoo) and curvature based (K-FAC). These methods can reach nearly identical training losses while producing weights with different spectra, representations, and performance. Recent studies have begun to identify optimizer-dependent feature and simplicity biases, including differences between Adam and GD in nonlinear models ( Cattaneo et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Xie and Li, 2024 ) and between spectral and Euclidean updates in deep linear networks ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) . These findings further motivate the central question we posed, and answering this requires distinguishing how quickly modes emerge from how they settle or disappear, since an optimizer can affect these phases differently. (a) GD (b) Muon (c) GD vs Muon: Birth and decay

Figure 1: Optimizer geometry sets the pace of spectral learning. In balanced aligned deep matrix factorization, GD and Muon produce distinct spectral learning trajectories (experimental details in App. F ). (a) Under GD, larger target modes are learned earlier, while smaller modes remain suppressed for longer. (b) Under Muon, factor amplitudes grow at a common speed, allowing smaller targets to reach full recovery earlier. (c) From the same initial amplitude 0.01 0.01 , Muon accelerates the growth of a positive target mode (red) and, importantly, removes the zero target mode in finite time (blue). GD instead exhibits delayed growth and slow decay. Thus, faster emergence of weak modes does not imply weaker removal of unsupported modes. Optimizer geometry determines which spectral components emerge, persist, and disappear. Other optimizers are discussed in later sections.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Figure 11: Optimization and rank dynamics in full observation matrix factorization. All optimizers train the same depth L = 8 L=8 deep linear factorization toward the same rank eight target and reach comparable final training loss. (a) GD (b) Adam (c) Muon (d) Shampoo (e) K-FAC (damped) Figure 12: Singular mode trajectories show optimizer dependent spectral clocks for L = 8 L=8 .

inspect:2611.06598.question: Across the LoRA fine-tuning experiments, how is behavioral compression rate measured, how do correction spectra predict it, and what matched-model, dataset, noise, and compression controls support the reported results?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. Most importantly, the same datasets exhibit substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models, showing that fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset–receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone. However, we show that correction spectra measured on the data are able to rank these rates within a receiver. Finally, we study a striking noise-reducing effect of compression: adapters trained on deliberately corrupted datasets fall far below the frozen model, yet after compression score above it (23.7% to 82.9% on GSM8K, against 77.6% for frozen Qwen2.5-7B), consistently across tested families and sizes. The damage is unevenly concentrated in the adapter’s leading singular directions, which compression appears to filter. Away from its training task, the compressed corrupted adapter also generalizes better than a clean fine-tune: on harder math it retains 97% of base accuracy, versus 44% for the clean adapter. Together, these results

raining task, the compressed corrupted adapter also generalizes better than a clean fine-tune: on harder math it retains 97% of base accuracy, versus 44% for the clean adapter. Together, these results suggest that the information cost of fine-tuning depends on the receiver, target behavior, and how the required corrections are represented in the learned update.

passages.section: 5.2 Damage Is Structured Across Adapter Directions
passages.text: The previous results suggest that the harmful and useful effects of the update are not uniformly distributed across its rank directions. We test this directly by decomposing corrupted adapters into singular directions and evaluating every contiguous window [ i , j ) [i,j) of the rank-16 update at full precision. Figure 5 reveals a consistent qualitative structure across model scales. Leading directions are strongly detrimental, an intermediate range contributes positively, and trailing directions have comparatively little effect. The location and width of these regimes vary across models, but the behavioral effect is clearly non-uniform across directions. This shows that the corruption is represented anisotropically within the learned update, and provides one mechanism by which compression can preferentially attenuate harmful behavior. The recovery controls above, however, show that directional selection alone does not account for the full effect. Figure 5: Corruption is structured across singular directions. (a) Accuracy relative to the frozen model for every contiguous window [ i , j ) [i,j) of singular directions retained at full precision. (b) Marginal contribution of each direction, computed by comparing windows that include it with those that do not.

passages.section: 5.2 Damage Is Structured Across Adapter Directions
passages.text: The effect is not restricted to a single model size or task. Additional experiments reproduce recovery across Qwen2.5 scales and other corrupted settings. On 72 off-task probes, the compressed corrupted adapter also remains closer to the frozen model than a clean fine-tune with comparable in-domain performance. Scaling, matched-norm, training-rank, cross-model, and off-task controls are reported in Appendix D . Together, these results show that compression need not merely degrade a fine-tuned update. When supervision induces both useful and harmful effects, those effects can be distributed very differently across the learned update, and aggressive bottlenecks can suppress them unequally. In the next section, we ask whether related properties of a successful update also predict how much rate is required to preserve its behavior.

We first test whether behavioral rate can be treated as an intrinsic property of the fine-tuning data. Figure 6 (b) measures R ⋆ ​ ( 0.90 ) R^{\star}(0.90) for the same three corpora across seven frozen receivers. The ordering changes with the receiver: XBRL tagging is the lowest-rate corpus for six receivers, but not for Qwen2.5-7B, where math is cheaper. Even closely related receivers can differ substantially: preserving 90% of the math gain requires 1.03 bits per value on Qwen2.5-Math-7B, compared with 0.41 on Qwen2.5-7B. Behavioral rate therefore depends on the dataset–receiver pair, rather than on the dataset alone. Section 4 motivates a receiver-relative statistic computed before training from the corrections requested by the data. We summarize the corresponding correction-gradient spectrum by its log-determinant (Appendix B.3 ). Within a fixed receiver, this quantity ranks behavioral rate well: across 24 arms and seven task families, Spearman correlation with R ⋆ ​ ( 0.90 ) R^{\star}(0.90) is ρ = 0.92 \rho=0.92 on Mistral-7B and ρ = 0.59 \rho=0.59 on Qwen2.5-7B, with a selection-adjusted permutation p = 0.0003 p=0.0003 (Figure 6 (a)). This association does not transfer reliably across receivers. After fixing the statistic, correlations on additional receiver panels are − 0.1 -0.1 on Llama-3.1-8B, − 0.4 -0.4 on Qwen3-8B, and + 0.1 +0.1 on a fresh Qwen2.5-7B panel. Corpus-only quantities and quantities obtained by scoring the corpus with the frozen model likewise fail to consistently order receivers. We therefore view correction spectra as informative within-receiver descriptors of compression difficulty, rather than as universal predictors of behavioral rate. Predicting R ⋆ R^{\star} from the data and receiver alone remains open.

Our experiments show that behavioral rate is receiver-relative: the same dataset can require different rates across frozen models, while parameter-space reconstruction error alone does not predict which compressed updates preserve behavior. At the same time, the success of the shrinkability approximation indicates that, once an update has been learned, much of its compression difficulty can be summarized by the behavioral response obtained when moving back along that update. Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, R ⋆ R^{\star} is an operational, codec-dependent rate rather than an information-theoretic optimum; different adapter parameterizations or codecs may induce different measured rates. Second, the correction-spectrum statistic is only a proxy for the full receiver-relative geometry and does not transfer reliably across receivers. Third, the shrinkability rule is supported by broad but retrospective evaluation, and remains to be validated prospectively on rates not observed when the rule is formulated. Finally, our recovery experiments use deliberately corrupted supervision to create a controlled mixture of useful and harmful effects. Whether the same structure governs naturally occurring fine-tuning errors remains an open question.

The ordering changes with the receiver: XBRL tagging is the lowest-rate corpus for six receivers, but not for Qwen2.5-7B, where math is cheaper. Even closely related receivers can differ substantially: preserving 90% of the math gain requires 1.03 bits per value on Qwen2.5-Math-7B, compared with 0.41 on Qwen2.5-7B. Behavioral rate therefore depends on the dataset–receiver pair, rather than on the dataset alone. Section 4 motivates a receiver-relative statistic computed before training from the corrections requested by the data. We summarize the corresponding correction-gradient spectrum by its log-determinant (Appendix B.3 ). Within a fixed receiver, this quantity ranks behavioral rate well: across 24 arms and seven task families, Spearman correlation with R ⋆ ​ ( 0.90 ) R^{\star}(0.90) is ρ = 0.92 \rho=0.92 on Mistral-7B and ρ = 0.59 \rho=0.59 on Qwen2.5-7B, with a selection-adjusted permutation p = 0.0003 p=0.0003 (Figure 6 (a)). This association does not transfer reliably across receivers. After fixing the statistic, correlations on additional receiver panels are − 0.1 -0.1 on Llama-3.1-8B, − 0.4 -0.4 on Qwen3-8B, and + 0.1 +0.1 on a fresh Qwen2.5-7B panel. Corpus-only quantities and quantities obtained by scoring the corpus with the frozen model likewise fail to consistently order receivers. We therefore view correction spectra as informative within-receiver descriptors of compression difficulty, rather than as universal predictors of behavioral rate. Predicting R ⋆ R^{\star} from the data and receiver alone remains open.

Our experiments show that behavioral rate is receiver-relative: the same dataset can require different rates across frozen models, while parameter-space reconstruction error alone does not predict which compressed updates preserve behavior. At the same time, the success of the shrinkability approximation indicates that, once an update has been learned, much of its compression difficulty can be summarized by the behavioral response obtained when moving back along that update. Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, R ⋆ R^{\star} is an operational, codec-dependent rate rather than an information-theoretic optimum; different adapter parameterizations or codecs may induce different measured rates. Second, the correction-spectrum statistic is only a proxy for the full receiver-relative geometry and does not transfer reliably across receivers. Third, the shrinkability rule is supported by broad but retrospective evaluation, and remains to be validated prospectively on rates not observed when the rule is formulated. Finally, our recovery experiments use deliberately corrupted supervision to create a controlled mixture of useful and harmful effects. Whether the same structure governs naturally occurring fine-tuning errors remains an open question.

candidates.title: How Finite-Rank Bottlenecks Shape the Low-Rank Adaptation Landscape
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the \emph{bottleneck rank}, rather than the sample size. candidates.title: The Behavioral Rate of Fine-Tuning: Compression as a Measure of Useful Information
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate $R^\star$ as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. candidates.title: A Riemannian Geometry for Low-rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is widely used as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique for pre-trained deep neural networks, which approximates the weight update via full fine-tuning by a low-rank matrix $BA^\top$. This parameterization leads to the equivalence relation $(B, A) \sim (BG^{-1}, AG^\top)$ for any invertible matrix $G$ because $BA^\top = BG^{-1}(AG^\top)^\top$ and thus both pairs yield the same loss value. This relation induces a quotient manifold where matrices $(BG^{-1}, AG^\top)$ for all $G$ are identified, eliminating redundant directions along which the loss value remains unchanged. To respect the geometry of this manifold, the original search space is endowed with a Riemannian metric that is invariant under the equivalence relation. Such a metric induces preconditioning at each gradient step and ensures that each weight update via LoRA changes the loss value, leading to efficient optimization. In this paper, we propose a new Riemannian metric that is specifically tailored to LoRA to close the gap to full fine-tuning at the weight level. candidates.title: Maximizing Capacity Utilization of LoRA Adapters for Mitigating the Learning-Forgetting Trade-off
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning-forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of $λ=0.01$ lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least $16$ relative to unpenalized LoRA.
